distillation_scope: Pure disease-name leaf distillation for the full clinical spectrum of acute liver failure. Etiologies such as acetaminophen, viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson disease, pregnancy-related disease, ischemia, and toxins are represented only as context, risk, axis, or treatment modifiers.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Observed or hidden exposure context that initiates acute hepatocyte injury: drug/toxin, viral, autoimmune, ischemic, pregnancy-related, metabolic, malignant infiltration, or indeterminate. This is a context gate, not a subtype in the disease name.

Rapid loss of hepatocyte mass through necrosis, apoptosis, mitochondrial injury, immune cytotoxicity, ischemia-reperfusion injury, or toxic metabolite injury. This drives aminotransferase rise and loss of functional reserve.

Impaired oxidative phosphorylation, beta-oxidation, glycogen handling, urea-cycle flux, and lactate clearance. Especially visible in hyperacute toxic, ischemic, mitochondrial, pregnancy-related, and pediatric phenotypes.

Necrotic liver releases DAMPs, cytokines, complement signals, and vasoactive mediators that produce SIRS, capillary leak, vasodilation, immune dysregulation, and susceptibility to infection even without an infectious etiology.

Failure to synthesize clotting factors, anticoagulant proteins, albumin, complement, and carrier proteins. INR and factor V rise/fall rapidly and are core likelihood axes; bleeding risk depends on rebalanced hemostasis, procedures, platelets, fibrinogen, and DIC context.
Acute hepatocyte and canalicular dysfunction impairs bilirubin conjugation/excretion and bile flow, producing jaundice, dark urine, pruritus in subacute cases, and rising total/direct bilirubin.

Loss of hepatic ammonia detoxification, altered amino-acid metabolism, lactate clearance failure, and systemic inflammation drive hepatic encephalopathy, seizures, cerebral edema, and intracranial hypertension.

Astrocyte swelling from glutamine/osmotic stress, cerebral hyperemia, inflammation, hyponatremia, seizure, and impaired autoregulation can produce raised intracranial pressure and herniation physiology.

Splanchnic vasodilation, capillary leak, hypovolemia, cytokine shock, renal vasoconstriction, ATN, hepatorenal physiology, acidosis, and electrolyte derangement produce AKI, shock, respiratory failure, DIC, and MODS.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Residual hepatocyte regeneration and recovery capacity
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Viable residual liver mass, preserved microcirculation, younger physiologic reserve, trigger withdrawal, and adequate support allow native recovery. Low activity means poor regeneration and higher transplant need.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Diverse acute liver insults converge on rapid hepatocyte death.
Toxic, ischemic, pregnancy-related, and metabolic contexts can directly impair hepatic energy metabolism.
Drug or toxin exposure increases the probability that the upstream ALF trigger is toxic.
Viral hepatitis serology/exposure context supports a viral upstream trigger.
Autoimmune markers and compatible course support immune-mediated hepatocyte injury.
Hemolysis, low ALP relative to bilirubin, and copper studies support Wilson-context ALF.
Hepatocyte necrosis releases AST.
Hepatocyte necrosis releases ALT.
Extensive necrosis and ischemic/toxic injury can raise LDH.
Necrotic liver releases inflammatory danger signals.
Loss of hepatocyte mass rapidly impairs factor synthesis.
Necroinflammation and canalicular dysfunction impair bile handling.
ALF impairs lactate clearance and energy metabolism.
Loss of glycogen stores and gluconeogenesis causes hypoglycemia.
Energetic failure produces clinically dangerous hypoglycemia.
Regenerating liver and renal tubular dysfunction can lower phosphate; severe hypophosphatemia affects muscle and cardiac function.
SIRS commonly causes leukocytosis, though infection and marrow context modulate it.
Inflammatory vasodilation and capillary leak can produce shock.
ALF immune paresis, invasive devices, and ICU exposure increase infection risk.
Reduced clotting-factor synthesis prolongs PT/INR.
Factor V reflects hepatic synthesis and is not corrected by vitamin K.
Albumin falls with impaired synthesis, dilution, inflammation, and chronic reserve.
Bleeding risk rises with severe coagulopathy, low fibrinogen, thrombocytopenia, invasive procedures, or DIC.
Severe ALF and shock can overlap with DIC physiology.
Bilirubin rises when excretion and conjugation fail.
Conjugated bilirubin rises with hepatocellular cholestasis.
Visible jaundice and scleral icterus track bilirubin burden.
Urea-cycle failure raises ammonia.
Hyperammonemia and inflammation drive encephalopathy.
ALF neurologic dysfunction is graded from mild confusion to coma.
Severe encephalopathy lowers GCS and triggers airway protection.
Hyperammonemia is a major driver of astrocyte swelling and cerebral edema.
Intracranial hypertension is the clinically dangerous cerebral edema state.
Cerebral edema and metabolic derangement can cause seizures.
TCD, ICP monitor, pupillary changes, or imaging may show intracranial hypertension.
Vasodilation, hypovolemia, and shock lower effective perfusion pressure.
ATN, hepatorenal physiology, pigment injury, or shock raises creatinine.
Renal dysfunction raises BUN, though hepatic urea-cycle failure can blunt it.
AKI is common in severe ALF and worsens ammonia, acid-base, and volume control.
Shock, lactate, renal failure, and mitochondrial dysfunction cause acidemia.
Metabolic acidosis lowers bicarbonate.
Coma, aspiration, ARDS, shock, and procedures can require intubation.
Regenerating hepatocytes restore factor synthesis.
Recovery and trigger control lower ongoing necrosis.
Improving native recovery lowers rescue transplant need.
Cerebral edema and herniation physiology are major early death pathways.
Shock, AKI, respiratory failure, and MODS dominate survival.
Native liver recovery reduces death and transplant need.

axes.shape_free_text: Exposure context for acetaminophen, idiosyncratic drug injury, herbal products, mushrooms, industrial toxins, or illicit/toxic co-ingestions.
History, medication record, serum level, adduct testing, or circumstantial evidence supporting acetaminophen exposure.
Measured serum acetaminophen concentration; can be low or absent in delayed or staggered overdose despite toxicity.
HAV, HBV, HEV, HSV, VZV, EBV, CMV, or other viral context from exposure, serology, PCR, or epidemiology.
HSV/VZV/CMV/EBV severe hepatitis context, especially pregnancy, immunosuppression, fever/leukopenia, mucocutaneous lesions, or PCR positivity.
Autoimmune hepatitis context from IgG, ANA/SMA/LKM/SLA, compatible biopsy, other autoimmune disease, or steroid-responsive course.
Wilson disease context from age, hemolysis, low ALP relative to bilirubin, low ceruloplasmin, copper studies, Kayser-Fleischer rings, or ATP7B testing.
Pregnancy or postpartum context for acute fatty liver of pregnancy, HELLP, herpes hepatitis, Budd-Chiari, or other pregnancy-modulated ALF.
Wild mushroom ingestion or amatoxin exposure context with delayed GI illness followed by hepatotoxicity.
Nausea, vomiting, poor intake, or early GI prodrome; common but nonspecific in ALF.
Right upper quadrant, epigastric, or diffuse abdominal discomfort from hepatic capsule stretch, toxin prodrome, viral hepatitis, biliary or ischemic context.
Visible jaundice, scleral icterus, dark urine, or acholic stool from bilirubin accumulation.
Hepatic or right upper quadrant tenderness from acute hepatitis, capsular stretch, congestion, or biliary overlap.
Enlarged palpable liver, imaging hepatomegaly, congestion, inflammation, infiltration, or Wilson/viral context.
Sleepiness, confusion, agitation, disorientation, psychomotor slowing, stupor, coma, or seizure attributable to hepatic encephalopathy or ALF-associated metabolic/ICP injury.
West Haven or clinically equivalent grade of hepatic encephalopathy in ALF; grade 3-4 indicates high cerebral edema and airway risk.
GCS decreases with severe encephalopathy, cerebral edema, intoxication, or airway-sedation context.
AST often rises into thousands in hyperacute toxic, ischemic, and viral ALF; lower values can occur in Wilson disease or late presentation.
ALT tracks hepatocellular injury and can rise into thousands; low ALT relative to bilirubin may occur in Wilson disease or late necrosis.
LDH rises with ischemic/toxic hepatocyte necrosis and hemolysis in Wilson-context ALF.
Total bilirubin can be modest in hyperacute acetaminophen/ischemic ALF and very high in viral, autoimmune, Wilson, or subacute ALF.
Direct bilirubin rises with hepatocellular cholestasis; unconjugated predominance can occur with hemolysis or impaired conjugation.
ALP is often normal or mildly elevated in hepatocellular ALF; very low ALP relative to bilirubin supports Wilson context, while high ALP suggests cholestatic or infiltrative context.
GGT may rise with cholestatic, alcohol, drug, or biliary context but is not required for ALF.
Core synthetic failure axis; INR >=1.5 with encephalopathy is central to ALF diagnosis and higher values signal transplant and bleeding/procedure risk context.
Hepatic synthetic marker not corrected by vitamin K; very low values mark severe ALF and transplant risk.
Albumin can fall with inflammation, dilution, capillary leak, subacute impaired synthesis, or underlying low reserve.
Ammonia elevation reflects detoxification failure and predicts cerebral edema risk, especially with high-grade encephalopathy.
Lactate rises from impaired hepatic clearance, mitochondrial failure, shock, seizure, or sepsis; persistent elevation worsens prognosis.
Acidemia from lactate, renal failure, shock, or toxin context; severe acidosis is a high-risk ALF feature.
Low bicarbonate reflects metabolic acidosis from lactate, renal dysfunction, toxin, seizure, or shock.
Hypoglycemia from impaired glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis is a dangerous ALF manifestation; stress hyperglycemia may coexist after dextrose or critical illness.
Hyponatremia worsens cerebral edema risk; hypernatremia may be induced therapeutically during ICP management.
Hypokalemia or hyperkalemia can occur from vomiting, renal failure, acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, dialysis, or replacement.
May fall during liver regeneration or tubular dysfunction and may rise with renal failure; severe derangement affects respiratory/cardiac muscle.
Creatinine rises with AKI, hepatorenal physiology, shock, rhabdomyolysis, toxin, or baseline CKD.
BUN can rise with AKI, bleeding, dehydration, or catabolism, but severe hepatic urea-cycle failure can blunt urea generation.
Leukocytosis or leukopenia reflects SIRS, infection, viral context, marrow reserve, steroid exposure, or stress response.
Anemia can reflect bleeding, dilution, chronic disease, hemolysis in Wilson context, or critical illness.
Platelets may fall from DIC, sepsis, hypersplenism, pregnancy-related disease, Wilson disease, dilution, or critical illness.
Fibrinogen can be low with DIC/consumption and bleeding risk, or preserved/high as an acute phase reactant.
D-dimer rises with DIC, thrombosis, inflammation, shock, pregnancy, or critical illness.
Perfusion pressure; low values reflect vasodilation, hypovolemia, sepsis, cardiogenic shock, sedation, or bleeding.
Hypoxemia from aspiration, ARDS, coma, shock, volume overload, or cardiopulmonary comorbidity.
Hazard of clinically significant cerebral edema, intracranial hypertension, or herniation physiology in ALF.
Hazard of seizure from cerebral edema, metabolic derangement, toxin, or withdrawal/co-ingestion context.
Hazard of clinically meaningful AKI or dialysis need during ALF.
Hazard of vasodilatory, hypovolemic, septic, hemorrhagic, or cardiogenic shock during ALF.
Hazard of DIC or clinically important consumptive coagulopathy overlapping ALF.
Hazard of major GI, intracranial, procedural, line-site, pulmonary, or mucosal bleeding in ALF context.
Hazard of intubation or mechanical ventilation for coma, airway protection, hypoxemia, ARDS, shock, or procedures.
Hazard of bacterial or fungal infection/sepsis during ALF from immune paresis, ICU care, invasive lines, aspiration, or immunosuppressive therapy.
Hazard of clinically dangerous hypoglycemia requiring continuous glucose monitoring and dextrose.
Hazard of dangerous arrhythmia from hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, acidosis, hypoglycemia, cardiomyopathy, or toxin context.
Evidence of active intracranial hypertension or cerebral edema from TCD, ICP monitoring, pupillary signs, imaging, or severe hyperammonemic coma.
Dialysis/CRRT need from AKI, hyperammonemia, acidosis, hyperkalemia, volume overload, or toxin clearance context.
Need for urgent transplant-center discussion or listing based on ALF severity, etiology, INR/lactate/ammonia, encephalopathy, acidosis, renal failure, cerebral edema, and regeneration failure.
Practical and medical feasibility of liver transplantation including donor availability, center access, contraindications, comorbidity, psychosocial status, malignancy, and patient preference.
Medical, oncologic, neurologic, active substance use, uncontrolled sepsis, cardiogenic shock, or social contraindication that may reduce transplant feasibility.
Feasibility of therapeutic plasma exchange based on vascular access, hemodynamics, blood-product availability, allergy, volume tolerance, and center capability.

Lifespan outcome hazard emerging from encephalopathy grade, cerebral edema, INR/factor V, lactate/acidosis, hypoglycemia, AKI, shock, infection, DIC/bleeding, etiology context, regeneration capacity, and transplant/support feasibility.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Aminotransferases rise together from hepatocellular injury, with ratios modulated by etiology.
Visible jaundice tracks bilirubin burden.
Higher INR contributes to bleeding/procedural risk, especially with low fibrinogen/platelets or DIC.
Hypofibrinogenemia amplifies bleeding risk.
Thrombocytopenia increases bleeding and procedure risk.
Ammonia contributes to encephalopathy, though inflammation/sedatives/toxins modulate exam findings.
High-grade encephalopathy increases cerebral edema and airway risk.
Marked hyperammonemia is a cerebral edema risk driver.
Hyponatremia worsens osmotic brain swelling in ALF.
Lactic acidosis lowers pH.
Persistent lactate reflects shock, mitochondrial failure, or poor clearance.
Rising creatinine indicates AKI severity.
Kidney failure reduces ammonia and acid-base control.
Shock worsens renal perfusion and ATN risk.
Consumptive coagulopathy increases bleeding risk.
Cerebral edema and herniation physiology can be rapidly fatal.
Shock drives multi-organ failure and death.
AKI worsens ammonia, acidosis, electrolyte, and volume control.
Sepsis is a major late death pathway and transplant barrier.
High transplant need reflects poor native recovery and high short-term risk.
Available rescue transplantation reduces mortality when native recovery is unlikely.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: NAC directly replenishes glutathione and supports acetaminophen detoxification.
Late presentation reduces antidote effect but does not eliminate supportive benefit.

failure_modes: uncontrolled cerebral edema or multi-organ failure

side_effects.interpretation: NAC can worsen nausea or vomiting.

treatments.context_specific_role: Antidotal and hepatoprotective vector field when acetaminophen or severe indeterminate ALF context is active.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Transplant pathway changes outcome only when severe ALF has meaningful transplant need.
Donor, center, medical, oncologic, neurologic, or psychosocial constraints can prevent transplant.
Severe cerebral edema can increase perioperative risk or become a contraindication.

side_effects.interpretation: Major surgery in coagulopathic ALF carries bleeding risk.
Post-transplant immunosuppression and ICU care increase infection risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rescue organ-replacement pathway when native recovery probability is inadequate and transplant is feasible.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: TPE requires access, replacement product, and hemodynamic tolerance.
TPE can remove copper and support coagulopathy in Wilson-context ALF.
When transplant is unavailable, liver-assist bridging may be more consequential.

side_effects.interpretation: Large volume exchange can cause instability.
Line placement and coagulopathy interact with plasma replacement.

treatments.context_specific_role: Liver-assist bridge for severe ALF or transplant-unavailable context; effect emerges through cytokine, toxin, ammonia, bilirubin, and coagulation axes.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: RRT is useful when kidney failure, ammonia, acidosis, hyperkalemia, toxin, or volume indication is active.

treatments.context_specific_role: Metabolic and renal bridge for hyperammonemia, acidosis, hyperkalemia, AKI, or toxin context.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Osmotherapy, sodium targeting, ventilation, positioning, sedation, and seizure control matter when cerebral edema risk is active.

side_effects.interpretation: Hyperosmolar therapy intentionally raises sodium but overcorrection can be harmful.

treatments.context_specific_role: Neurocritical vector field for high-grade encephalopathy, cerebral edema, seizure, or intracranial hypertension.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Perfusion support matters when shock or hypoperfusion physiology is active.

side_effects.interpretation: Lines and ICU support can increase infection exposure.
Over-resuscitation can worsen pulmonary edema or oxygenation.

treatments.context_specific_role: Perfusion bridge that reduces shock, lactate, AKI, and downstream mortality while causal hepatic recovery or transplant path is determined.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Dextrose support directly prevents hypoglycemic neurologic injury.

treatments.context_specific_role: Metabolic bridge preventing hypoglycemia, arrhythmia, and muscle/respiratory complications while ALF trajectory evolves.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Transfusion and factor support are most useful for active bleeding or invasive procedures.
Ongoing consumption can rapidly erase correction.

side_effects.interpretation: Transfusion-associated volume overload or lung injury can impair oxygenation.

treatments.context_specific_role: Hemostatic support when bleeding, procedure, or consumptive coagulopathy context is active; not a standalone cure for ALF.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Antimicrobials and source evaluation change outcome when infection is present or strongly suspected.
Immunosuppression for autoimmune context increases infection surveillance importance.

treatments.context_specific_role: Infection-control vector field for ALF immune paresis or documented/suspected sepsis, not an ALF diagnosis label.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Acyclovir targets HSV/VZV replication, not non-herpes ALF.

side_effects.interpretation: Acyclovir crystal nephropathy risk increases with renal dysfunction or dehydration.

treatments.context_specific_role: Etiology-directed antiviral vector when herpesvirus ALF context is active.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Steroids target immune-mediated hepatocyte injury.
Active infection can worsen with corticosteroids.

treatments.context_specific_role: Etiology-directed immune vector when autoimmune hepatitis context is active and infection risk is managed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Copper removal and chelation target Wilson-context ALF.
Rescue non-transplant therapy becomes more important when transplant is unavailable.

side_effects.interpretation: Chelation can cause marrow toxicity in susceptible patients.

treatments.context_specific_role: Copper-removal and chelation vector for Wilson-context ALF; context axis prevents use as a generic ALF treatment.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Delivery or obstetric source control applies to AFLP/HELLP/pregnancy-related contexts.

side_effects.interpretation: Delivery or surgery in ALF/coagulopathy can increase bleeding risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Pregnancy-context source control rather than a generic ALF label.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises toxic-context prior and makes NAC response more active; hyperacute cases may have very high AST/ALT with relatively modest bilirubin early.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Medication or toxin context is directly observed.
Toxic and ischemic ALF often produce very high aminotransferases.
Hyperacute acetaminophen ALF can have lower bilirubin early than viral/subacute ALF.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: NAC directly targets acetaminophen toxic metabolism and supports hepatic perfusion/oxidative stress.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises viral-context prior; HAV/HEV/HBV often have high bilirubin and INR, while HSV may have fever, leukopenia, pregnancy/immunosuppression context, and very high aminotransferases.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Serology/PCR/exposure context is directly observed.
Viral ALF often produces marked jaundice.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: Acyclovir is mechanism-linked to herpesvirus replication, not all viral ALF.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises autoimmune-context prior; response depends on how much necrosis is already irreversible and whether infection is present.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Autoimmune markers, IgG, biopsy, and course define context.
Immunosuppression increases infection risk.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: Steroids target immune-mediated injury when active.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises Wilson-context prior; bilirubin and hemolysis can be high while AST/ALT and ALP are relatively low.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Copper studies, hemolysis, and low ALP/bilirubin ratio identify context.
Coombs-negative hemolysis can be severe.
Disproportionately low ALP supports Wilson-context ALF.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: Copper removal and chelation target this context.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises pregnancy-related ALF context and changes available interventions and bleeding risk.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Pregnancy/postpartum status is directly observed.
HELLP/AFLP contexts may include thrombocytopenia.
Delivery and coagulopathy increase bleeding risk.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: Obstetric source control applies only to pregnancy-related contexts.

present.trajectory_modulation: Allows necrosis, hyperammonemia, renal injury, and cerebral edema to accumulate before effective therapy.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Uncontrolled injury worsens synthetic failure.
Detoxification failure accumulates.
Delayed control increases high-grade encephalopathy and ICP risk.
Delayed therapy worsens survival.

present.trajectory_modulation: Does not define ALF etiology, but worsens renal, cardiopulmonary, infection, and transplant reserve.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Lower renal reserve increases AKI risk.
Older/frail patients have more infection complications.
Comorbidities can reduce transplant feasibility.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises concern for acute-on-chronic liver failure rather than pure ALF; background bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelets, and encephalopathy must be interpreted against baseline.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Chronic liver disease can raise bilirubin before acute injury.
Baseline coagulopathy can pre-exist ALF.
Portal hypertension can lower platelets.

present.trajectory_modulation: Does not change ALF diagnosis but removes a major rescue vector field when native recovery fails.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Feasibility constraint is directly observed.
High transplant need plus infeasibility worsens survival.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: The rescue pathway cannot be delivered when feasibility is low.
Bridge/support therapies become more relevant when transplant is unavailable.

supportive_care: Treat ALF as an ICU and transplant-center emergency: repeat neurologic exam, INR/PT, factor V when available, AST/ALT, bilirubin fractions, ammonia, lactate, glucose, electrolytes, creatinine/BUN, CBC, fibrinogen, D-dimer, ABG/VBG, and urine output frequently during the first 24-72 hours.

Preserve etiology evidence as context axes: acetaminophen history/level, viral serology/PCR, autoimmune markers, pregnancy/postpartum status, copper studies, toxin/mushroom exposure, ischemic/shock context, malignancy/infiltration, and medication/herbal exposure.

Do not use final pathology, final paper diagnosis, transplant histology, or response to a specific treatment as ordinary ranking evidence; keep them as confirmatory/context evidence with use_in_ranking:false in cases.

Monitor and manage cerebral edema risk: head elevation, avoid hyponatremia, maintain perfusion, treat fever/seizure/hypoxia/hypoglycemia, and use hypertonic saline or mannitol when active intracranial hypertension context is present.
Use continuous glucose monitoring or frequent bedside glucose checks; prevent hypoglycemia while avoiding large untracked swings in sodium and osmolality.
Correct coagulopathy for active bleeding or invasive procedures; do not treat INR alone as if it were ordinary anticoagulation because ALF hemostasis is rebalanced and dynamic.
Assess infection actively with cultures and imaging when clinically indicated; ALF can have SIRS without infection, but immune paresis and ICU devices make infection a major event hazard.
Use renal replacement therapy when AKI, hyperammonemia, acidosis, hyperkalemia, toxin clearance, or volume status activates the corresponding axes.

Transplant path, plasma exchange, NAC, acyclovir, corticosteroids, copper removal/chelation, and obstetric source control should be selected by context axes and forward outcome simulation rather than first-line labels.
When chronic liver disease is present, avoid double counting: interpret baseline bilirubin/INR/albumin/platelets by background or an acute-on-chronic manifold rather than forcing pure ALF semantics.
quality_notes: The disease-specific medical input used for this distillation is only the disease name: Acute liver failure.
Exactly one derived_hazard axis is present: mortality_hazard_in_D-ACUTE-LIVER-FAILURE.
Etiologies are represented as risk/context/treatment modifier axes and do not appear in disease_name.
No prohibited treatment-ranking label keys are used.
All treatment trajectory_modifications are dictionaries keyed by mechanism or axis id.
All risk_factors modulation fields are dictionaries.
